items.question: What primitive types does TypeScript have, and how does number differ from C#?
items.answer: TypeScript has string, number, boolean, and bigint. Unlike C# which offers int, long, double, and decimal as separate types, TypeScript's number is always IEEE 754 double-precision floating point — the same as JavaScript. There is no built-in decimal type. For money, store integer cents or use a decimal library. bigint handles integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
followUps: When would you use bigint over number?
items.sixtySeconds: string, number, boolean, bigint. number is double like JS. No decimal — use cents or a library. bigint for huge IDs.

items.question: What is the difference between null, undefined, void, and never?
items.answer: null means intentional absence of value. undefined means not yet assigned or property missing. void is the return type of functions whose result you should ignore — at run time it is undefined. never is the bottom type representing values that cannot exist — used for functions that always throw, infinite loops, and exhaustive switch checks. With strictNullChecks, null and undefined require explicit union types.
followUps: How does strictNullChecks compare to C# nullable reference types?
Show an exhaustive switch with never.
items.sixtySeconds: null intentional, undefined missing. void for ignored returns. never for impossible paths and exhaustiveness. strictNullChecks makes absence explicit.

items.question: Explain the difference between any, unknown, and never.
items.answer: any is the escape hatch that disables type checking — assignable to and from everything, contagious to downstream code. unknown accepts any value but requires narrowing (typeof, instanceof, guards, or schema validation) before use — preferred at API boundaries like JSON.parse. never is the bottom type — no value satisfies it. Use unknown at boundaries, never for exhaustiveness, and avoid any in production code.
followUps: How would you safely type JSON.parse?
How does any compare to C# dynamic?
items.sixtySeconds: any turns off checking. unknown must be narrowed. never is bottom type. Use unknown at boundaries, ban any in new code.

items.question: What are literal types and what does as const do?
items.answer: Literal types narrow primitives to exact values: "pending" instead of string, 42 instead of number. const declarations infer literal types automatically; let widens to the base type. as const is a postfix assertion that freezes an object or array to its deepest readonly literal values. Derive union types from as const objects: type Status = typeof STATUS[keyof typeof STATUS]. This replaces enums with zero run-time overhead.
followUps: What is the difference between const and as const?
How do literal types enable discriminated unions?
items.sixtySeconds: const keeps literals. as const deep-freezes objects. Derive unions from const objects. Foundation for discriminated unions.

items.question: When do you use type versus interface?
items.answer: Use type for unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, and utility-type compositions. Use interface for object shapes, especially when classes implement them, interfaces extend each other, or you need declaration merging (e.g. augmenting Window in a .d.ts file). Both are erased at run time. TypeScript uses structural typing — shape matters, not the declaration name.
followUps: Can you use interface for a union type?
items.sixtySeconds: type for unions and complex types. interface for object contracts and merging. Both compile away. Structural typing.

items.question: Should you use TypeScript enums or literal unions?
items.answer: Prefer literal unions and as const objects for new code. Numeric enums generate a run-time IIFE object with reverse mapping — poor tree-shaking and JSON can deliver invalid numbers. String enums are better but still emit objects. const enums are inlined but have isolatedModules compatibility issues. Literal unions have zero run-time cost, are JSON-friendly, and work with exhaustiveness checking via never. Use enums only when interoping with C# backends that serialize numeric enums.
followUps: What is reverse mapping in numeric enums?
items.sixtySeconds: Unions + as const for new code. Enums generate run-time objects. Validate deserialized enum values. String enums better than numeric.

items.question: How do TypeScript basic types map to C# built-in types?
items.answer: int/long/byte map to number or bigint. decimal has no TS equivalent — serialize as string or integer cents. double/float map to number (same IEEE 754). bool maps to boolean. char maps to a single-character string. string maps to string (C# reference type, TS primitive). C# null maps to TS null; missing optional properties map to undefined. C# enums deserialize as numbers — validate range. All TS types erase at compile time unlike C# CLR types.
followUps: How do you safely transfer decimal currency?
Does strictNullChecks prevent null at run time?
items.sixtySeconds: One number type in TS. No decimal. Types erase. Two absent values. Validate enums and decimals at API boundaries.

items.question: Do TypeScript types exist at run time?
items.answer: No. TypeScript performs compile-time type checking and then erases all type annotations when emitting JavaScript. const x: number = 42 becomes const x = 42. There is no run-time type information, no reflection on types, and no protection against malformed JSON. You must validate external data with schema libraries (Zod, Valibot) or manual guards. This is fundamentally different from C# where CLR types exist at run time with metadata and reflection support.
followUps: What tools validate JSON at run time in TypeScript?
items.sixtySeconds: Types erase at emit. No run-time checking. Validate JSON with Zod or guards. Unlike C# CLR metadata.
